subject: Biology
title: Discovery of the Cell
summary: In 1665 a thin slice of cork showed tiny boxes Robert Hooke called cells. Then came living cells (1674) and the nucleus (1831).
keyPoints: **1665, Robert Hooke:** cork, honeycomb-like boxes, named **cells** (Latin cella, a small room).
Hooke's cork cells were **dead**: only cell walls.
**1674, Leeuwenhoek:** first **living** cells, in pond water.

blocks.alt: Hooke's drawing of cork from Micrographia
blocks.caption: Hooke's own drawing of cork (Micrographia, 1665).

blocks.alt: Diagram of empty cork cells with cell walls
blocks.caption: Empty boxes: the walls of dead cells.

sections.h: 1674 and 1831: living cells and the nucleus

blocks.p: With better lenses, **Antonie van Leeuwenhoek** saw free, moving cells in a drop of **pond water** in 1674. In 1831 **Robert Brown** found a round, dense body in orchid cells: the **nucleus**.

blocks.alt: A living cell with nucleus, cytoplasm and membrane
blocks.caption: A living cell is not empty: it has a control centre.
From cork to the cell theory.
